oi_lesson.objective: Understand how the electrical spike travels continuously down the axon without losing strength.
oi_lesson.why_it_matters: In living brain tissue and lab-grown brain organoids, signals must travel over long distances without fading. Knowing how this happens helps engineers design better ways to send commands to lab-grown neural networks.
prerequisites: Brain cells maintain a resting voltage using charged particles.
Neurons have long wire-like extensions called axons.
oi_lesson.simple_explanation: Imagine a row of falling dominoes. When the first domino falls, it knocks over the next one, and that one knocks over the next, keeping the push just as strong at the end of the line as it was at the start. An electrical signal in a brain cell works the same way: one spot opening its gates triggers the next spot to do the exact same thing.
step_by_step: A trigger near the cell body causes tiny gate openings in the cell wall at the start of the axon.
Positively charged particles rush inside, flipping the local voltage from negative to positive.
This sudden local change forces the adjacent gates just a bit further down the axon to pop open.
The wave moves forward step by step, while the previous spots quickly reset themselves so the signal only travels in one direction.
oi_lesson.technical_depth: This self-propagating wave relies on voltage-gated ion channels. As sodium channels open and depolarize one patch of membrane, the electrical shift spreads locally to trigger neighboring voltage-gated channels. Refractory periods ensure unidirectional propagation by temporarily disabling channels that just fired.

misconceptions.misconception: Electricity flows through an axon just like a metal wire.
misconceptions.correction: Unlike metal wires that passively let current fade over distance, axons actively regenerate the electrical signal at every tiny section so it stays strong.

knowledge_check.question: Does an action potential fade as it travels down a long axon?
knowledge_check.answer: No, because each section of the axon regenerates the signal freshly.

knowledge_check.question: What prevents the signal from running backward toward the cell body?
knowledge_check.answer: A resting recovery period behind the moving wave keeps the gates temporarily locked.

knowledge_check.question: What opens the gates further down the axon?
knowledge_check.answer: The electrical change from the active spot right next to them.

oi_lesson.exercise: Draw a straight line representing an axon. Mark five sequential spots. Write down how a positive charge entering spot one triggers spot two, repeating the process down the line.
oi_lesson.summary: Signals travel down axons through a chain-reaction wave where each section of the cell wall freshly regenerates the electrical spike.

bci_lesson.objective: Understand how EEG electrodes pick up electrical signals, why reference electrodes are needed to measure voltage differences, and the role of ground electrodes in safety and noise reduction.
bci_lesson.why_it_matters: Brain signals are extremely small voltage fluctuations measured relative to another point on the body. Without a proper reference and ground system, electrical noise from the environment would completely drown out the brain's signals.
prerequisites: Basic electrical concepts like voltage, which is the difference in electrical charge between two points.
The understanding that neurons generate tiny electrical currents that travel through tissue and bone.
bci_lesson.simple_explanation: Imagine measuring the height of a hill. You cannot just state a number without deciding where sea level is—your reference point. In EEG, sensors cannot read an absolute brain signal on their own. Instead, they measure the difference in electrical activity between a sensor on the scalp and a sensor placed on a neutral spot like the earlobe or mastoid bone. Meanwhile, a ground electrode acts as a safety shield, draining away unwanted electrical interference from things like nearby lamps or wall power.
step_by_step: 1. Electrical Contact: A conductive gel or paste is applied to the scalp to help pass tiny brain signals from the skin into the metal EEG electrode.
2. Differential Measurement: The recording hardware constantly compares the voltage at a scalp electrode against the voltage at a reference electrode.
3. Grounding: A separate ground electrode absorbs stray environmental electrical noise, helping the recording system ignore outside interference.
bci_lesson.technical_depth: EEG amplifiers use differential amplifiers to measure the voltage difference between an active recording electrode and a reference electrode ($V_{active} - V_{reference}$). Common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR) is the hardware's ability to cancel out signals that appear identically at both inputs, such as 50 or 60 Hz line noise from wall power. The ground electrode sets the patient's body electrical potential relative to the amplifier, keeping the signals within the safe operating range of the hardware.
misconceptions: Misconception: An EEG electrode measures the absolute electrical charge of a single brain area. Fact: It always measures a relative voltage difference between two specific physical points.
Misconception: The ground electrode records brain waves. Fact: The ground electrode is strictly for safety and noise stabilization and does not contribute to the brain signal data.

knowledge_check.question: What does an EEG electrode actually measure?
knowledge_check.answer: It measures the voltage difference between a scalp location and a reference point.

knowledge_check.question: Why is a ground electrode important?
knowledge_check.answer: It helps stabilize electrical potential and reduces environmental noise like power line interference.

knowledge_check.question: Can you have an EEG recording without a reference electrode?
knowledge_check.answer: No, voltage is always a measurement of the difference between two points, requiring at least one reference.

bci_lesson.exercise: Draw a simple diagram showing a scalp electrode, a reference electrode placed on an earlobe, and a differential amplifier calculating the difference between them.
bci_lesson.summary: EEG electrodes capture minute scalp voltages, which are only meaningful when compared against a reference electrode. A ground electrode protects the user and helps filter out external electrical noise.

internship.topic: Microcontroller peripherals: GPIO, timers, PWM and interrupts
internship.explanation: Microcontroller peripherals are hardware tools built inside the chip that help it talk to the outside world without constantly wasting the main processor's time. GPIO means General Purpose Input and Output, used to read buttons or blink LEDs. Timers count internal clock ticks to measure time accurately. PWM, or Pulse Width Modulation, rapidly turns a pin on and off to control motor speed or dim lights. Interrupts act like a doorbell, pausing the main code instantly when an important external event happens, such as a sensor signal.
internship.practical_example: Imagine building a robotic arm in an internship project. You use a GPIO pin to read a safety button, a timer to schedule sensor readings every 10 milliseconds, PWM to control the grip motor speed, and an interrupt to instantly stop the arm if an emergency bumper is pressed.
internship.exercise: Write down how you would configure a timer and an interrupt to make a robot's status LED flash every second without using a blocking delay function in your main loop.
internship.model_answer: I would set up a hardware timer to generate an interrupt overflow every one second. Inside the interrupt service routine, I would toggle the state of the GPIO pin connected to the LED, keeping the main loop free for other tasks.
internship.why_it_works: Using hardware timers and interrupts avoids wasting processor cycles on waiting loops, ensuring your robot stays responsive to critical sensor inputs.
internship.improvement_tip: Keep your interrupt service routines extremely short and fast, setting a flag variable instead of doing heavy math inside the interrupt itself.
